These are, perhaps, not the very best times for humanities majors. Seldom do we even hear the once-standard defense that, by pursuing a course of study in subjects of that kind, students “learn how to think.” Such a justification still points to real value, at least in the most demanding settings. Take Harvard’s course Humanities 10, whose digital device-free environment and syllabus covering everything from The Odyssey and Ulysses to Plato and James Baldwin — at a pace of one substantial book per week — recently drew the attention of the Wall Street Journal. Yet it’s always been true that you don’t have to major in anything to learn how to think, or in any case, to make a start of doing so.

Take the philosophy-and-literature YouTuber Jared Henderson, who in the video at the top of the post tells us how he began his self-directed study in high school. “I did what a lot of people would think is natural,” he says. “I went to a bookstore, and then I just found some books that I wanted to read.” The pieces of light reading he took home: Friedrich Nietzsche’s The Birth of Tragedy and Martin Heidegger’s Introduction to Metaphysics.

“If you know anything about philosophy, I think you know that that was probably not the ideal way to start.” But all the years of learning and teaching since have finally put him in a position of knowing how to begin, and in the span of half an hour, he lays out an intellectual roadmap for anyone in the same position as his teenage self, with stops in logic, metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and political philosophy.

That sequence reflects the reasonable assumption that, before we can evaluate arguments about how society ought to be arranged, we must learn to evaluate statements about how things are. We must, in other words, learn how to think — but also learn about the nature of reality itself, and how or whether we can know anything about it in the first place, questions relevant to both metaphysics and epistemology. That may seem like a daunting task, but Henderson frames all its stages in relation to one another, naming some of the most famous philosophers who have written in the relevant fields along the way. No single reading could give you mastery of their work, or even a full understanding of it, however clear the bigger picture might seem. But the attempt teaches the true first lesson of philosophy: in one area of knowledge or another, you’ll always be a beginner.
